claim: Mutations in the inositol 5-phosphatase OCRL cause Lowe syndrome and Dent's disease.
source: Mutations in the inositol 5-phosphatase OCRL cause Lowe syndrome and Dent's disease.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction (Attree et al., 1992; Hoopes et al., 2005).

claim: OCRL is a direct clathrin interactor.
source: Although OCRL, a direct clathrin interactor, is recruited to late-stage clathrin-coated pits, clinical manifestations have been primarily attributed to intracellular sorting defects.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by previous studies cited in the manuscript (Ungewickell et al., 2004; Choudhury et al., 2005).

claim: OCRL is recruited to late-stage clathrin-coated pits.
source: Although OCRL, a direct clathrin interactor, is recruited to late-stage clathrin-coated pits, clinical manifestations have been primarily attributed to intracellular sorting defects.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 2E-G showing sequential recruitment of SNX9 and OCRL at endocytic clathrin-coated pits.

claim: OCRL loss in Lowe syndrome patient fibroblasts impacts clathrin-mediated endocytosis and results in an endocytic defect.
source: Here we show that OCRL loss in Lowe syndrome patient fibroblasts impacts clathrin-mediated endocytosis and results in an endocytic defect.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4 showing decreased turnover of endocytic clathrin-coated pits and delayed transferrin endocytosis in patient cells.

claim: Lowe syndrome patient cells exhibit an accumulation of clathrin-coated vesicles.
source: These cells exhibit an accumulation of clathrin-coated vesicles and an increase in U-shaped clathrin-coated pits, which may result from sequestration of coat components on uncoated vesicles.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data in Figure 4H showing increased numbers of clathrin-coated vesicles in patient cells.

claim: Lowe syndrome patient cells exhibit an increase in U-shaped clathrin-coated pits.
source: These cells exhibit an accumulation of clathrin-coated vesicles and an increase in U-shaped clathrin-coated pits, which may result from sequestration of coat components on uncoated vesicles.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data in Figure 4H showing increased numbers of U-shaped pits in patient cells.

claim: The accumulation of clathrin-coated vesicles and U-shaped pits may result from sequestration of coat components on uncoated vesicles.
source: These cells exhibit an accumulation of clathrin-coated vesicles and an increase in U-shaped clathrin-coated pits, which may result from sequestration of coat components on uncoated vesicles.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed data, supported by the finding of increased particulate clathrin in patient cells (Figure 5H-I).

claim: Endocytic vesicles that fail to lose their coat nucleate the majority of the numerous actin comets present in patient cells.
source: Endocytic vesicles that fail to lose their coat nucleate the majority of the numerous actin comets present in patient cells.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5 showing clathrin, AP-2, SNX9, and transferrin at the tips of actin comets, and Figure 6 showing progressive loss of comets upon plasma membrane PI(4,5)P2 depletion.

claim: SNX9 is an adaptor that couples late-stage endocytic coated pits to actin polymerization.
source: SNX9, an adaptor that couples late-stage endocytic coated pits to actin polymerization and which we found to bind OCRL directly, remains associated with such vesicles.
evidence: This is supported by previous literature (Yarar et al., 2007) cited in the manuscript.

claim: SNX9 binds OCRL directly.
source: SNX9, an adaptor that couples late-stage endocytic coated pits to actin polymerization and which we found to bind OCRL directly, remains associated with such vesicles.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments in Figure 2B-D and GST pulldown experiments in Figure 2D.

claim: SNX9 remains associated with endocytic vesicles that fail to lose their coat in patient cells.
source: SNX9, an adaptor that couples late-stage endocytic coated pits to actin polymerization and which we found to bind OCRL directly, remains associated with such vesicles.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5C-E showing SNX9 at the tips of actin comets in patient cells.

claim: OCRL acts as an uncoating factor.
source: These results indicate that OCRL acts as an uncoating factor and that defects in clathrin-mediated endocytosis likely contribute to pathology in patients with OCRL mutations.
evidence: This is inferred from the accumulation of clathrin-coated vesicles in patient cells (Figure 4H) and the delayed turnover of clathrin coats (Figure 4A-G).

claim: Defects in clathrin-mediated endocytosis likely contribute to pathology in patients with OCRL mutations.
source: These results indicate that OCRL acts as an uncoating factor and that defects in clathrin-mediated endocytosis likely contribute to pathology in patients with OCRL mutations.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the observed endocytic defects in patient cells.

claim: Lowe syndrome is characterized by congenital cataracts, renal proximal tubule dysfunction, cognitive disabilities and developmental delay.
source: Lowe syndrome is characterized by congenital cataracts, renal proximal tubule dysfunction, cognitive disabilities and developmental delay (Delleman et al., 1977; Kenworthy and Charnas, 1995; Böckenhauer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: Patients with Dent's disease exhibit similar proximal tubule defects but no, or only mild, additional clinical defects.
source: Patients with Dent's disease exhibit similar proximal tubule defects but no, or only mild, additional clinical defects (Bökenkamp et al., 2009; Shrimpton et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: OCRL has a modular structure comprised of an N-terminal PH domain followed by an unstructured amino acid stretch, the 5-phosphatase domain, an ASH domain and a catalytically-inactive RhoGAP-like domain.
source: OCRL has a modular structure that is comprised of an N-terminal PH domain (Mao et al., 2009) followed in sequence by an unstructured amino acid stretch, the 5-phosphatase domain, an ASPM-SPD2-Hydin (ASH) domain and a catalytically-inactive RhoGAP-like domain (Ponting, 2006; Erdmann et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: OCRL is expressed in all tissues.
source: OCRL is expressed in all tissues and has a broad subcellular distribution, which is mediated by interactions with proteins that control membrane traffic and the actin cytoskeleton.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is established knowledge about OCRL expression.

claim: OCRL has a broad subcellular distribution mediated by interactions with proteins that control membrane traffic and the actin cytoskeleton.
source: OCRL is expressed in all tissues and has a broad subcellular distribution, which is mediated by interactions with proteins that control membrane traffic and the actin cytoskeleton.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by the list of OCRL interactors cited.

claim: OCRL interacts with clathrin-heavy chain, the clathrin adaptor AP-2, Rab and Rho family GTPases and the endosomal adaptors APPL1 and Ses1/2.
source: These include clathrin-heavy chain, the clathrin adaptor AP-2, Rab and Rho family GTPases and the endosomal adaptors APPL1 and Ses1/2 (Ungewickell et al., 2004; Choudhury et al., 2005, 2009; Shin et al., 2005; Hyvola et al., 2006; Lichter-Konecki et al., 2006; Erdmann et al., 2007; Fukuda et al., 2008; Swan et al., 2010; Dambournet et al., 2011; Noakes et al., 2011; Pirruccello et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: OCRL has been localized to the Golgi complex, to a variety of endosomal compartments as well as to clathrin-coated pits.
source: Consistent with such interactions, OCRL has been localized to the Golgi complex, to a variety of endosomal compartments as well as to clathrin-coated pits (Olivos-Glander et al., 1995; Dressman et al., 2000; Ungewickell et al., 2004; Choudhury et al., 2005; Faucherre et al., 2005; Hyvola et al., 2006; Erdmann et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations to localization studies.

claim: INPP5B does not bind clathrin and AP-2.
source: INPP5B, a 5-phosphatase very similar to OCRL, has many of the same properties, but does not bind clathrin and AP-2, and correspondingly is not localized at endocytic clathrin-coated pits (Erdmann et al., 2007; Williams et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: INPP5B is not localized at endocytic clathrin-coated pits.
source: INPP5B, a 5-phosphatase very similar to OCRL, has many of the same properties, but does not bind clathrin and AP-2, and correspondingly is not localized at endocytic clathrin-coated pits (Erdmann et al., 2007; Williams et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 and PI(3,4,5)P3 are the two preferred substrates of OCRL.
source: PI(4,5)P2 and PI(3,4,5)P3, the two preferred substrates of OCRL, are primarily concentrated in the plasma membrane, where they help define its identity.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is established knowledge about OCRL substrate specificity.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 and PI(3,4,5)P3 are primarily concentrated in the plasma membrane.
source: PI(4,5)P2 and PI(3,4,5)P3, the two preferred substrates of OCRL, are primarily concentrated in the plasma membrane, where they help define its identity.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is established knowledge about phosphoinositide localization.

claim: The pathological manifestations of Lowe syndrome and Dent's disease are thought to arise from abnormal protein sorting and membrane recycling.
source: The pathological manifestations of Lowe syndrome and Dent's disease are thought to arise from abnormal protein sorting and membrane recycling (Erdmann et al., 2007; Swan et al., 2010; Vicinanza et al., 2011; Mehta et al., 2014), as loss of OCRL would disrupt the appropriate coordination between membrane progression and changes in phosphoinositide composition.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Nucleation and expansion of endocytic clathrin coats requires PI(4,5)P2 at the plasma membrane.
source: Nucleation and expansion of endocytic clathrin coats requires PI(4,5)P2 at the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is established knowledge about clathrin-mediated endocytosis.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 represents a critical co-receptor for all the clathrin adaptors.
source: PI(4,5)P2 represents a critical co-receptor for all the clathrin adaptors (Di Paolo and De Camilli, 2006; Mettlen et al., 2009; Sun et al., 2007; Traub, 2009) and its levels (controlled by dynamic turnover) impact the lifetime of clathrin-coated pits (Zoncu et al., 2007; Nakatsu et al., 2010; Antonescu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 levels impact the lifetime of clathrin-coated pits.
source: PI(4,5)P2 represents a critical co-receptor for all the clathrin adaptors (Di Paolo and De Camilli, 2006; Mettlen et al., 2009; Sun et al., 2007; Traub, 2009) and its levels (controlled by dynamic turnover) impact the lifetime of clathrin-coated pits (Zoncu et al., 2007; Nakatsu et al., 2010; Antonescu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Coat shedding (uncoating) after the endocytic reaction requires PI(4,5)P2 dephosphorylation.
source: Conversely, coat shedding (uncoating) after the endocytic reaction requires PI(4,5)P2 dephosphorylation, as first revealed by studies of clathrin-mediated endocytosis in axon terminals (Cremona et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Absence of synaptojanin 1 results in a striking accumulation of clathrin-coated vesicles.
source: Absence of synaptojanin 1, the most abundant 5-phosphatase in the synapse, results in a striking accumulation of clathrin-coated vesicles (Cremona et al., 1999; Harris et al., 2000; Verstreken et al., 2003; Milosevic et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: There is evidence that PI(4,5)P2 dephosphorylation may assist in the fission reaction of endocytosis.
source: There is also evidence that PI(4,5)P2 dephosphorylation may assist in the fission reaction of endocytosis (Stefan et al., 2002; Rusk et al., 2003; Mani et al., 2007; Sun et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2009; Chang-Ileto et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: OCRL has a role in preventing the accumulation of PI(4,5)P2 on post-endocytic membranes.
source: While it has been shown that OCRL has a role in preventing the accumulation of PI(4,5)P2 on post-endocytic membranes (Vicinanza et al., 2011), there is no evidence to date that the absence of OCRL, or defects in OCRL function, impairs clathrin-mediated endocytosis.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: There is no evidence to date that the absence of OCRL, or defects in OCRL function, impairs clathrin-mediated endocytosis.
source: While it has been shown that OCRL has a role in preventing the accumulation of PI(4,5)P2 on post-endocytic membranes (Vicinanza et al., 2011), there is no evidence to date that the absence of OCRL, or defects in OCRL function, impairs clathrin-mediated endocytosis.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: Mass spectrometry analysis confirmed clathrin heavy and light chain as major hits in OCRL immunoprecipitates.
source: Mass spectrometry further confirmed clathrin heavy and light chain as major hits in the immunoprecipitates and revealed additional specific OCRL interactors (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1A,B.

claim: OCRL interactors include subunits of the endocytic clathrin adaptor AP-2, Rab proteins and Ses1/2.
source: These included known binding partners of OCRL, such as subunits of the endocytic clathrin adaptor AP-2, Rab proteins and Ses1/2 but, surprisingly, not APPL1.
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1A,B.

claim: APPL1 was not detected in OCRL immunoprecipitates.
source: These included known binding partners of OCRL, such as subunits of the endocytic clathrin adaptor AP-2, Rab proteins and Ses1/2 but, surprisingly, not APPL1.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on the mass spectrometry data.

claim: APPL1 was possibly outcompeted by Ses1/2, which bind to the same site in OCRL but with a higher affinity.
source: Possibly APPL1 was outcompeted by Ses1/2, which bind to the same site in OCRL but with a higher affinity (Swan et al., 2010; Noakes et al., 2011; Pirruccello et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the absence of APPL1, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Proteins that participate in clathrin-dependent transport steps featured particularly prominently in the OCRL interactome.
source: Proteins that participate in clathrin-dependent transport steps featured particularly prominently in the OCRL interactome.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on the mass spectrometry data shown in Supplementary file 1A,B.

claim: AP-2, EpsinR (CLINT1), SNX9 and PI3KcIIα showed the highest enrichment in OCRL immunoprecipitates by western blotting.
source: In addition to clathrin, interactors such as AP-2, EpsinR (CLINT1), SNX9 and PI3KcIIα showed the highest enrichment by western blotting (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The cation-independent mannose 6-phosphate receptor (CI-M6PR) was confirmed in OCRL immunoprecipitates by western blotting but was not as enriched as other interactors.
source: The cation-independent mannose 6-phosphate receptor (CI-M6PR), a cargo protein for clathrin-coated pits whose transport was previously shown to be affected by OCRL knockdown (Vicinanza et al., 2011), was also confirmed by western blotting, but was not as enriched (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: EpsinR, SNX9 and PI3KcIIα are all known clathrin interactors.
source: Clathrin and AP-2 are known to bind OCRL directly, while EpsinR, SNX9 and PI3KcIIα are all known clathrin interactors (Gaidarov et al., 2001; Lundmark and Carlsson, 2003; Mills et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A substantial overlap was observed between major OCRL interactors and proteins previously identified in a mass spectrometry analysis of clathrin binding partners.
source: In fact, a substantial overlap was observed between major OCRL interactors revealed by our experiments and proteins previously identified in a similar mass spectrometry analysis of clathrin binding partners (Hubner et al., 2010) as well as in a global analysis of clathrin-coated vesicles (Blondeau et al., 2004; Borner et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Loss of clathrin and AP-2 binding in OCRLX3 was accompanied by the loss of CI-M6PR, EpsinR and PI3KcIIα in anti-GFP-OCRLX3 immunoprecipitates.
source: Western blot analysis revealed that loss of clathrin and AP-2 binding was accompanied by the loss of CI-M6PR, EpsinR and PI3KcIIα in the anti-GFP-OCRLX3 immunoprecipitates (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The interaction of OCRL with SNX9 was not abolished by mutations in clathrin and AP-2 binding sites.
source: In contrast, the interaction of OCRL with SNX9, which also contains binding sites for clathrin and for AP-2 (Lundmark and Carlsson, 2003), was not abolished by the three mutations in OCRL (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: SNX9 binds other proteins implicated in the late stages of clathrin-mediated endocytosis, such as dynamin, synaptojanin and N-WASP, through an N-terminal SH3 domain.
source: SNX9 binds other proteins implicated in the late stages of clathrin-mediated endocytosis, such as dynamin, synaptojanin and N-WASP, through an N-terminal SH3 domain that recognizes proline-rich motifs with the canonical PxxP sequence (Figure 2A; Badour et al., 2007; Lundmark and Carlsson, 2003; Mayer, 2001; Yeow-Fong et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: OCRL contains a PxxP site (175REPPPPP181) in the predicted unfolded region that connects its N-terminal PH domain to its central inositol 5-phosphatase domain.
source: OCRL contains a PxxP site (175REPPPPP181) in the predicted unfolded region that connects its N-terminal PH domain to its central inositol 5-phosphatase domain (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: GFP-OCRLWT co-enriched endogenous SNX9, while a GFP-OCRL mutant lacking the PxxP motif (GFP-OCRLP3) failed to co-precipitate SNX9.
source: Anti-GFP immunoprecipitation of cell extracts expressing GFP-OCRLWT co-enriched endogenous SNX9, while a GFP-OCRL mutant in which three prolines (P177, 178, and 181) of the PxxP motif were mutated to alanine (GFP-OCRLP3), failed to co-precipitate SNX9 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: GFP-SNX9WT but not a GFP-SNX9 construct lacking the SH3 domain (GFP-SNX9ΔSH3) co-precipitated endogenous OCRL.
source: Conversely, GFP-SNX9WT but not a GFP-SNX9 construct lacking the SH3 domain (GFP-SNX9ΔSH3) co-precipitated endogenous OCRL (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The PxxP motif in OCRL is necessary for the interaction with SNX9.
source: Therefore, we concluded that the PxxP motif in OCRL is necessary for the interaction with SNX9.
evidence: This is concluded from the co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 2B-C.

claim: SNX18 is a close paralogue of SNX9 with partially overlapping functions.
source: A close paralogue of SNX9 with partially overlapping functions is SNX18 (Park et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Anti-GFP immunoprecipitations from cells expressing a GFP fusion of SNX18 also recovered endogenous OCRL.
source: Anti-GFP immunoprecipitations from cells expressing a GFP fusion of SNX18 also recovered endogenous OCRL (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both GST-OCRL217 and GST-OCRL176 recovered clathrin from mouse brain lysates.
source: Both fragments contained a previously described clathrin box (73LIDIA77) (Mao et al., 2009) and each recovered clathrin, as expected (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by GST pulldown data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Only the OCRL217 fragment containing the PxxP motif pulled down SNX9 from mouse brain lysates.
source: However, only the OCRL217 fragment containing the PxxP motif pulled down SNX9 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by GST pulldown data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: SNX9 directly binds OCRL via an interaction of its SH3 domain with the PxxP site in OCRL.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that SNX9 directly binds OCRL via an interaction of its SH3 domain with the PxxP site in OCRL.
evidence: This is concluded from the co-immunoprecipitation and GST pulldown experiments shown in Figure 2B-D.

claim: In the great majority of cases (93.18 ± 1.25%), the peak of OCRL fluorescence lagged slightly behind that of SNX9 at endocytic clathrin-coated pits.
source: In the great majority of cases (93.18 ± 1.25%; n = 150 events, 3 independent experiments), the peak of OCRL fluorescence lagged slightly behind that of SNX9, suggesting a very late function of OCRL in clathrin-mediated budding (Figure 2E–G; Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2E-G and Video 1.

claim: The sequential recruitment of SNX9 followed by OCRL suggests a very late function of OCRL in clathrin-mediated budding.
source: In the great majority of cases (93.18 ± 1.25%; n = 150 events, 3 independent experiments), the peak of OCRL fluorescence lagged slightly behind that of SNX9, suggesting a very late function of OCRL in clathrin-mediated budding (Figure 2E–G; Video 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal recruitment data shown in Figure 2E-G.

claim: Patient cells lack OCRL.
source: Patient cells lack OCRL, as indeed confirmed by immunofluorescence (Figure 3A,B) and western blotting (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3A-B and western blot data in Figure 3C.

claim: A near 1.5-fold increase in the steady state levels of PI(4,5)P2 was observed in patient cells.
source: Accordingly, a near 1.5-fold increase in the steady state levels of PI(4,5)P2 was also observed in these cells as expected (Figure 3D; Zhang et al., 1998; Wenk et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by HPLC analysis data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Patient cells show enhanced punctate immunoreactivity for clathrin, AP-2, and SNX9.
source: Immunofluorescence for endogenous clathrin and AP-2 showed a robust increase of their punctate immunoreactivity in patient cells (Figure 3E–H). An even more striking increase was observed for SNX9 puncta (Figure 3I–J) (see also below).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3E-J.

claim: Clathrin-coated pits showed a clustered distribution in patient cells.
source: Additionally, clathrin-coated pits showed a clustered distribution.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on immunofluorescence observations in Figure 3E-J.

claim: Exogenous overexpression of GFP-OCRLWT rescued the clathrin phenotype in patient cells.
source: Exogenous overexpression of GFP-OCRLWT rescued this phenotype (Figure 3K–K′), while expression of a catalytically inactive OCRL (GFP-OCRLD523G) failed to do so (Figure 3L–L′).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3K-L′.

claim: Expression of catalytically inactive OCRL (GFP-OCRLD523G) failed to rescue the clathrin phenotype in patient cells.
source: Exogenous overexpression of GFP-OCRLWT rescued this phenotype (Figure 3K–K′), while expression of a catalytically inactive OCRL (GFP-OCRLD523G) failed to do so (Figure 3L–L′).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3K-L′.

claim: Patient cells show a significant increase in the number of long-lived clathrin-coated pits and a reduction of short-lived ones.
source: In patient cells, the turnover of clathrin-coated pits was reduced, as revealed by a significant increase in the number of long-lived pits and a reduction of short-lived ones (short: 22.3%, medium: 42.3%, long: 35.4%) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by TIRF microscopy data and lifetime analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Re-expression of wild type OCRL rescued the clathrin-coated pit lifetime phenotype in patient cells.
source: This phenotype was rescued by the re-expression of wild type OCRL (short: 33.8%, medium: 49.9%, long: 16.3%) (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by TIRF microscopy data and lifetime analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In control cells, GFP-OCRLWT was recruited to clathrin spots as the clathrin fluorescence started to diminish.
source: In control cells, GFP-OCRLWT was recruited to clathrin spots as the clathrin fluorescence started to diminish (Figure 4D; Video 2), in agreement with previous observations (Erdmann et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by spinning disk confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4D and Video 2.

claim: In patient cells, the dynamics of clathrin-coated pits were disrupted, as demonstrated by the longer persistence of the clathrin signal.
source: In patient cells, the dynamics of the pits were disrupted, as demonstrated by the longer persistence of the clathrin signal (Figure 4E; Video 3).
evidence: This is supported by spinning disk confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4E and Video 3.

claim: GFP-OCRLWT restored normal clathrin turnover in patient cells.
source: GFP-OCRLWT restored normal clathrin turnover in these cells (Figure 4F; Video 4), while GFP -OCRLD523G failed to do so despite being recruited to the pits and remaining associated with them (Figure 4E; Video 3).
evidence: This is supported by spinning disk confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4F and Video 4.

claim: GFP-OCRLD523G failed to restore normal clathrin turnover in patient cells despite being recruited to the pits and remaining associated with them.
source: GFP-OCRLWT restored normal clathrin turnover in these cells (Figure 4F; Video 4), while GFP -OCRLD523G failed to do so despite being recruited to the pits and remaining associated with them (Figure 4E; Video 3).
evidence: This is supported by spinning disk confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4E and Video 3.

claim: Delayed turnover in patient cells resulted in an increase in the number of clathrin puncta that were positive for GFP-OCRLD523G at any given time.
source: Delayed turnover in patient cells resulted in an increase in the number of clathrin puncta (mRFP-tagged CLC) that were positive for GFP-OCRLD523G at any given time (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by colocalization analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Electron microscopy revealed a prominent increase of wide-neck (primarily U-shaped) pits and of free clathrin-coated vesicles in the cortical region of patient cells.
source: This analysis confirmed the global increase in the number of clathrin-coated endocytic profiles and, in particular, a prominent increase of wide-neck (primarily U-shaped) pits and of free clathrin-coated vesicles in the cortical region of the cell (less than 500 nm from the plasma membrane, that is clathrin-coated vesicles most likely of endocytic origin) (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The loss of OCRL impairs uncoating.
source: These results suggest that the loss of OCRL impairs uncoating, a finding consistent with its very late recruitment at pits.
evidence: This is inferred from the accumulation of clathrin-coated vesicles and U-shaped pits shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The absence of OCRL delays late steps in clathrin-mediated endocytosis, possibly as a result of sequestration of endocytic factors on uncoated vesicles.
source: Its absence also delays late steps in clathrin-mediated endocytosis, possibly as a result of sequestration of endocytic factors on uncoated vesicles.
evidence: This is inferred from the lifetime analysis data in Figure 4A-C and the accumulation of clathrin-coated vesicles in Figure 4H.

claim: Confocal microscopy revealed a delay in the shift of transferrin fluorescence from the cell surface to deeper positions in the cytoplasm in patient cells compared to control fibroblasts.
source: Confocal microscopy of cells pre-incubated with fluorescent transferrin revealed a delay in the shift of fluorescence from the cell surface to deeper positions in the cytoplasm in patient cells compared to control fibroblasts (Figure 4I–J).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4I-J.

claim: Biochemical measurement confirmed a defect in the uptake of biotinylated transferrin in patient cells.
source: This defect was quantified and confirmed biochemically by measuring the uptake of biotinylated transferrin at various time points during a 20-min time course (Figure 4K).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA-based assay data shown in Figure 4K.

claim: Biotin labeling showed accumulation of the endogenous surface pool of the transferrin receptor at the plasma membrane in patient cells compared to controls.
source: In addition, biotin labeling of the endogenous surface pool of the transferrin receptor showed its accumulation at the plasma membrane in patient cells compared to controls (Figure 4L).
evidence: This is supported by biotinylation assay data shown in Figure 4L.

claim: OCRL is required for normal dynamics of clathrin-mediated endocytosis.
source: From these results, we conclude OCRL is required for normal dynamics of clathrin-mediated endocytosis.
evidence: This is concluded from the collective data on clathrin-coated pit dynamics and transferrin uptake shown in Figure 4.

claim: A reported phenotype of Lowe syndrome patient fibroblasts is an abnormal organization of actin, with the presence of numerous actin comets.
source: A reported phenotype of Lowe syndrome patient fibroblasts is an abnormal organization of actin, with the presence of numerous actin comets (Suchy and Nussbaum, 2002; Allen, 2003; Hayes et al., 2009; Cui et al., 2010; Dambournet et al., 2011; Vicinanza et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Analysis of F-actin revealed a reduction in the number of actin stress fibers, with the prominent accumulation of peripheral actin foci and actin comets in patient cells.
source: Accordingly, analysis of F-actin in control and patient cells using either phalloidin (in fixed cells) or mCherry-CHUTR (in live cells) (Burkel et al., 2007) revealed a reduction in the number of actin stress fibers, with the prominent accumulation of peripheral actin foci and actin comets (also referred to as actin tails) in patient cells (Figure 5A–B; Video 5).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 5A-B and Video 5.

claim: Actin comets in patient cells are dependent on N-WASP and the Arp2/3 complex.
source: These comets, which are dependent on N-WASP and the Arp2/3 complex (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–F), are thought to reflect the nucleation of actin on intracellular vesicles that ectopically accumulate PI(4,5)P2 due to the lack of OCRL (Vicinanza et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-F.

claim: Expression of GFP-OCRLWT suppressed the actin comets in patient cells.
source: Consistent with this possibility, expression of GFP-OCRLWT suppressed the comets (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G–I′), while expression of catalytically-inactive GFP-OCRLD523G localized to the head of the comets but failed to rescue this phenotype (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1J–J′; Video 6).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G-I′.

claim: Expression of catalytically-inactive GFP-OCRLD523G localized to the head of the comets but failed to rescue the actin comet phenotype.
source: Consistent with this possibility, expression of GFP-OCRLWT suppressed the comets (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G–I′), while expression of catalytically-inactive GFP-OCRLD523G localized to the head of the comets but failed to rescue this phenotype (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1J–J′; Video 6).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1J-J′ and Video 6.

claim: Nearly every actin tail propelled vesicles positive for clathrin, AP-2, SNX9, SNX18, PI3KcIIα, and transferrin.
source: Further analysis of proteins at the head of the comets revealed the presence of late-stage endocytic clathrin coat components and their accessory factors, including clathrin, AP-2, SNX9, SNX18, and PI3KcIIα, as well as transferrin, a known cargo of clathrin-mediated endocytosis (Figure 5C; Video 7). Nearly every actin tail propelled vesicles positive for these proteins (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 5C-D and Video 7.

claim: Endogenous SNX9 and clathrin light chain immunoreactivity were present at the tips of comets labeled by phalloidin.
source: This was also the case for endogenous proteins, as revealed by the presence of SNX9 and clathrin light chain immunoreactivity at the tips of comets labeled by phalloidin (an F-actin marker) (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The tips of actin comets were mostly devoid of endosomal markers, such as Rab5 or the FYVE domain of HRS.
source: The tips of these comets however, were mostly devoid of endosomal markers, such as Rab5 or the FYVE domain of HRS (Figure 5—figure supplement 1K–L).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1K-L.

claim: The levels of SNX9 were strikingly increased in patient cells.
source: The levels of SNX9 were strikingly increased in patient cells (Figure 5F–G), possibly due to its accumulation and thus sequestration at comet tips.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5F-G.

claim: The increase in SNX9 levels may be due to its accumulation and sequestration at comet tips.
source: The levels of SNX9 were strikingly increased in patient cells (Figure 5F–G), possibly due to its accumulation and thus sequestration at comet tips.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the increased SNX9 levels.

claim: The overall cellular levels of clathrin and AP-2 were similar in control and patient cells.
source: In contrast, the overall cellular levels of clathrin and AP-2 were similar in control and patient cells (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: An increase in the pool of assembled clathrin coats in patient cells was demonstrated biochemically.
source: However, an increase in the pool of assembled clathrin coats in patient cells was demonstrated biochemically (Figure 5H–I).
evidence: This is supported by subcellular fractionation data shown in Figure 5H-I.

claim: Homogenization of cells followed by high-speed centrifugation revealed an increased fraction of clathrin heavy chain in the particulate fraction of patient cells.
source: Homogenization of cells under conditions known to preserve assembled clathrin, followed by high-speed centrifugation to yield cytosol (C) and total particulate (P) fractions, revealed an increased fraction of clathrin heavy chain in the particulate fraction of patient cells (Figure 5H–I).
evidence: This is supported by subcellular fractionation data shown in Figure 5H-I.

claim: The coat and cargo of the intracellular actin-propelled vesicles are very similar to those of endocytic clathrin-coated pits.
source: Thus, the coat and cargo of the intracellular actin-propelled vesicles are very similar to those of endocytic clathrin-coated pits.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of clathrin, AP-2, SNX9, and transferrin at comet tips shown in Figure 5C-E.

claim: Vesicles at comet tips are endocytic clathrin-coated vesicles whose coat failed to shed due to the lack of OCRL catalytic activity.
source: This supports the idea that vesicles at comet tips are endocytic clathrin-coated vesicles whose coat failed to shed due to the lack of OCRL catalytic activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the collective data on comet composition and the rescue by wild-type but not catalytically inactive OCRL.

claim: A small subset of vesicles driving the comets were larger than would be expected from endocytic clathrin-coated vesicles and may represent micropinosomes.
source: A small subset of vesicles driving the comets were larger than would be expected from endocytic clathrin-coated vesicles and may represent micropinosomes.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observation of larger vesicles.

claim: Knockdown of SNX9 revealed a decrease in the number of endogenous comets observed in patient cells.
source: Given the striking increase of SNX9 levels in patient cells and its known role in coordinating clathrin-coated pits maturation with actin nucleation (Yarar et al., 2007), we explored its importance in the formation of actin tails. Knockdown of SNX9 followed by immunostaining with phalloidin revealed a decrease in the number of endogenous comets observed in patient cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by siRNA knockdown and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-C.

claim: Most of the remaining SNX9 puncta observed in cells after knockdown associated with the tips of the comets.
source: Importantly, most of the remaining SNX9 puncta observed in cells after knockdown associated with the tips of the comets (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The interaction between SNX9 and OCRL may help coordinate actin polymerization at late stage clathrin-coated pits with the turnover of PI(4,5)P2.
source: These results suggest that the interaction between SNX9 and OCRL may help coordinate actin polymerization at late stage clathrin-coated pits with the turnover of PI(4,5)P2.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the SNX9 knockdown results.

claim: The recruitment of OCRL to clathrin-coated pits was not dependent on its interaction with SNX9.
source: The recruitment of OCRL to clathrin-coated pits was not dependent on its interaction with SNX9, however. This was evidenced by the expression of an SNX9-binding mutant construct of OCRL (GFP-OCRLP3) that still localized to clathrin-coated pits in patient cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Multiple binding partners likely regulate OCRL recruitment to clathrin-coated pits.
source: Given the interactions of OCRL with several prominent endocytic factors such as clathrin and AP-2, it is highly likely that multiple binding partners regulate its recruitment to clathrin-coated pits.
evidence: This is inferred from the known interactions of OCRL with multiple endocytic proteins.

claim: Selective depletion of plasma membrane PI(4,5)P2 via activation of M1 muscarinic acetylcholine receptor resulted in progressive disappearance of actin comets.
source: If actin comets are in fact nucleated by plasma membrane-derived PI(4,5)P2 still present on uncoated endocytic vesicles due to the absence of OCRL, depletion of plasma membrane PI(4,5)P2 should result in their progressive disappearance. Alternatively, if comets are generated by the synthesis of PI(4,5)P2 on intracellular structures, depletion of plasma membrane PI(4,5)P2 would not affect them. In order to discern between these two scenarios, we selectively depleted PI(4,5)P2 at the plasma membrane via the activation of a PLC-coupled receptor, the M1 muscarinic acetylcholine receptor (M1R).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6A-D and Video 8.

claim: Prior to OxoM addition, GFP-PHPLCδ was selectively localized at the plasma membrane.
source: Prior to OxoM addition, GFP-PHPLCδ was selectively localized at the plasma membrane, as typically observed for this PI(4,5)P2 biosensor in resting cells (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The addition of OxoM triggered PLC-mediated PI(4,5)P2 hydrolysis, resulting in the relocation of GFP-PHPLCδ to the cytosol.
source: The addition of OxoM triggered PLC-mediated PI(4,5)P2 hydrolysis into IP3 and diacyl glycerol, which resulted in the relocation of GFP-PHPLCδ to the cytosol, indicating PI(4,5)P2 depletion at the plasma membrane (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 depletion correlated with a transient increase of cytosolic Ca2+.
source: This change correlated with a transient increase of cytosolic Ca2+, as expected (Figure 6C; Horowitz et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by GCaMP3 fluorescence data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The transient increase in cytosolic Ca2+ led to a massive transient depolymerization of actin, including actin comets.
source: In turn, this led to a massive transient depolymerization of actin, including actin comets, and a sharp increase in the diffuse cytosolic fluorescence of the actin reporter, mCherry-CHUTR (Figure 6B–D).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6B-D.

claim: As Ca2+ levels reverted to the baseline level, actin comets reformed.
source: Subsequently, as Ca2+ levels reverted to the baseline level (Figure 6C), actin comets reformed (Figure 6B–D), often reemerging at sites where they had previously disappeared (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6B-D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Actin comets often reemerged at sites where they had previously disappeared, suggesting that vesicles driving the comets had retained actin-nucleating properties during the transient actin depolymerization.
source: Subsequently, as Ca2+ levels reverted to the baseline level (Figure 6C), actin comets reformed (Figure 6B–D), often reemerging at sites where they had previously disappeared (Figure 6—figure supplement 1). This suggested that vesicles driving the comets had retained actin-nucleating properties during the transient actin depolymerization.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that comets reemerge at the same locations shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the continued presence of OxoM, reappearance of the comets after the Ca2+-induced actin depolymerization was followed by their progressive loss.
source: In the continued presence of OxoM (conditions where plasma membrane PI(4,5)P2 remains depleted), reappearance of the comets after the Ca2+-induced actin depolymerization was followed by their progressive loss (Figure 6B,D; Video 8).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6B,D and Video 8.

claim: Termination of the OxoM signal by addition of atropine led to the rapid reformation of PI(4,5)P2 at the plasma membrane and to a striking progressive recovery of the number of new comets.
source: Termination of the OxoM signal by addition of its antagonist, atropine, led to the rapid reformation of PI(4,5)P2 at the plasma membrane (Figure 6A) and to a striking progressive recovery of the number of new comets rocketing throughout the cytosol (Figure 6B,D; Video 8).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6A-B,D and Video 8.

claim: The bulk of the vesicles found at the tip of actin comets are newly formed endocytic vesicles originating from the plasma membrane.
source: These results are consistent with the idea that the bulk of the vesicles found at the tip of actin comets are newly formed endocytic vesicles originating from the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is inferred from the progressive loss of comets upon plasma membrane PI(4,5)P2 depletion and their recovery upon PI(4,5)P2 reformation shown in Figure 6.

claim: The PI(4,5)P2 probe GFP-PHPLCδ was infrequently detected at the tip of comets.
source: The observations described thus far suggest a scenario in which the lack of OCRL-mediated PI(4,5)P2 hydrolysis results in a delay of endocytosis and impaired uncoating of endocytic clathrin-coated vesicles. They further suggest that coated PI(4,5)P2-rich vesicles drive actin nucleation. This hypothesis, however, contrasts with the very infrequent detection of the PI(4,5)P2 probe, GFP-PHPLCδ, at the tip of comets (Figure 7A, inset).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Images through the middle of the cell revealed the robust presence of PI(4,5)P2 at the plasma membrane but not intracellularly.
source: This was particularly evident in images through the middle of the cell revealing the robust presence of PI(4,5)P2 at the plasma membrane but not intracellularly (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Even a higher sensitivity probe, consisting of two tandem PH domains of PLCδ (GFP-2XPHPLCδ) yielded similar results.
source: Even a higher sensitivity probe, consisting of two tandem PH domains of PLCδ (GFP-2XPHPLCδ) yielded similar results.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on observations with the higher sensitivity probe.

claim: The difference in GFP-PHPLCδ labeling of comet tips and of the plasma membrane was striking on images of the bottom plane of a cell showing intracellular comets that encountered the plasma membrane and evaginated it into filopodia-like structures.
source: The difference in GFP-PHPLCδ labeling of comet tips and of the plasma membrane was even more striking on images of the bottom plane of a cell showing intracellular comets that encountered the plasma membrane and evaginated it into filopodia-like structures, akin to those generated by Listeria-driven comets (Figure 7B,D; Video 9).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 7B,D and Video 9.

claim: The heavy labeling of the plasma membrane of filopodia encapsulating the actin comet stood in striking contrast to the lack of labeling (or very weak labeling) of the vesicle at the tip of the comet.
source: In this case, the heavy labeling of the plasma membrane of filopodia encapsulating the actin comet stood in striking contrast to the lack of labeling (or very weak labeling) of the vesicle at the tip of the comet.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on observations in Figure 7B,D.

claim: Overexpression of PIPK1γ along with GFP-PHPLCδ and mCherry-CHUTR in control human fibroblasts led to a robust formation of actin comets.
source: Since these results brought into question the presence of PI(4,5)P2 at the tips of comets, we examined the localization of the PI(4,5)P2 probe in an additional cellular model of PI(4,5)P2-dependent actin comet formation, the overexpression of a PI4P 5-kinase. Overexpression of one such enzyme, PIPkinase type-1-gamma (PIPK1γ), along with GFP-PHPLCδ and mCherry-CHUTR in control human fibroblasts cells led to a robust formation of actin comets (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–A″).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-A″.

claim: Even in cells overexpressing PIPK1γ, detection of GFP-PHPLCδ labeling at the tips of the comets was inconsistent, in contrast to the robust labeling of the plasma membrane.
source: Even in this case, where the intracellular pool of PI(4,5)P2 was dramatically expanded, detection of GFP-PHPLCδ labeling at the tips of the comets (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B) was inconsistent (although more frequently observed than in Lowe syndrome patient cells), in contrast to the robust labeling of the plasma membrane (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C–C‴).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B-C‴.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 may be present at a much lower concentration on the vesicles than on the plasma membrane, but these low levels may be sufficient to nucleate actin.
source: This finding could have three non-mutually exclusive explanations: (1) PI(4,5)P2 may be present at a much lower concentration on the vesicles than on the plasma membrane, but these low levels may be sufficient to nucleate actin, (2) GFP-PHPLCδ may be a better reporter of plasma membrane PI(4,5)P2 given the presence of a yet unidentified PHPLCδ co-receptor only on this membrane; (3) PI(4,5)P2 present on the vesicles may be shielded and possibly sequestered by actin and actin regulatory proteins.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the lack of PHPLCδ labeling at comet tips.

claim: GFP-PHPLCδ may be a better reporter of plasma membrane PI(4,5)P2 given the presence of a yet unidentified PHPLCδ co-receptor only on this membrane.
source: This finding could have three non-mutually exclusive explanations: (1) PI(4,5)P2 may be present at a much lower concentration on the vesicles than on the plasma membrane, but these low levels may be sufficient to nucleate actin, (2) GFP-PHPLCδ may be a better reporter of plasma membrane PI(4,5)P2 given the presence of a yet unidentified PHPLCδ co-receptor only on this membrane; (3) PI(4,5)P2 present on the vesicles may be shielded and possibly sequestered by actin and actin regulatory proteins.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the lack of PHPLCδ labeling at comet tips.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 present on the vesicles may be shielded and possibly sequestered by actin and actin regulatory proteins.
source: This finding could have three non-mutually exclusive explanations: (1) PI(4,5)P2 may be present at a much lower concentration on the vesicles than on the plasma membrane, but these low levels may be sufficient to nucleate actin, (2) GFP-PHPLCδ may be a better reporter of plasma membrane PI(4,5)P2 given the presence of a yet unidentified PHPLCδ co-receptor only on this membrane; (3) PI(4,5)P2 present on the vesicles may be shielded and possibly sequestered by actin and actin regulatory proteins.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the lack of PHPLCδ labeling at comet tips.

claim: In patient cells overexpressing M1R and treated with OxoM, several vesicles became positive for GFP-PHPLCδ during the period of actin depolymerization that accompanied the transient rise in cytosolic Ca2+.
source: One observation favoring the idea that actin and actin regulatory proteins may shield/sequester PI(4,5)P2 came from patient cells overexpressing M1R and treated with OxoM. In such cells, several vesicles became positive for GFP-PHPLCδ during the period of actin depolymerization that accompanied the transient rise in cytosolic Ca2+ (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: GFP-PHPLCδ was rapidly displaced by mCherry-CHUTR as actin comets reformed.
source: However, GFP-PHPLCδ was rapidly displaced by mCherry-CHUTR as actin comets reformed, providing further evidence for the presence of PI(4,5)P2 on internal vesicles in Lowe syndrome patient cells (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: OCRL acts at late-stage clathrin-coated pits to dephosphorylate PI(4,5)P2 and facilitates the shedding of endocytic factors.
source: Overall, these findings support a model in which OCRL acts at late-stage clathrin-coated pits to dephosphorylate PI(4,5)P2 and facilitates the shedding of endocytic factors (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a model inferred from the collective data presented in the study.

claim: In the absence of OCRL, the accumulation of PI(4,5)P2-rich vesicles that fail to lose their clathrin coat leads to an endocytic defect resulting from the sequestration of endocytic factors on these vesicles.
source: In the absence of OCRL, as in Lowe syndrome, the accumulation of PI(4,5)P2-rich vesicles that fail to lose their clathrin coat leads to an endocytic defect resulting from the sequestration of endocytic factors on these vesicles (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a model inferred from the collective data presented in the study.

claim: A role of PI(4,5)P2 dephosphorylation in the normal progression of clathrin-mediated endocytosis was first described at neuronal synapses.
source: A role of PI(4,5)P2 dephosphorylation in the normal progression of clathrin-mediated endocytosis was first described at neuronal synapses, where studies of synaptojanin 1 emphasized an uncoating function of this protein (Cremona et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Dephosphorylation of PI(4,5)P2 in the membranes of the budding vesicles was proposed to act as a mechanism to generate a line tension at the vesicle neck.
source: Subsequent work in a variety of model systems supported this idea but also suggested a role of this phosphoinositide in the late stages of endocytosis. Dephosphorylation of PI(4,5)P2 in the membranes of the budding vesicles was proposed to act as a mechanism to generate a line tension at the vesicle neck (Stefan et al., 2002; Rusk et al., 2003; Mani et al., 2007; Sun et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2009; Chang-Ileto et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Progression through the late stages of endocytosis could be affected by the sequestration of endocytic proteins on PI(4,5)P2-rich uncoated vesicles.
source: Progression through the late stages of endocytosis could be also affected by the sequestration of endocytic proteins on PI(4,5)P2-rich uncoated vesicles, as postulated for synapses lacking synaptojanin 1 or all three endophilins (Mani et al., 2007; Milosevic et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The present study demonstrates a defect of endocytosis in Lowe syndrome patient fibroblasts.
source: The present study demonstrates a defect of endocytosis in Lowe syndrome patient fibroblasts.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the data presented in the study.

claim: The endocytic defect in patient cells is characterized by an accumulation of late-stage (primarily U-shaped) endocytic clathrin-coated pits and by a delay in the internalization of transferrin.
source: This defect is characterized by an accumulation of late-stage (primarily U-shaped) endocytic clathrin-coated pits and by a delay in the internalization of transferrin, a clathrin-coated pit cargo.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the data in Figure 4.

claim: The results point to a defect in clathrin uncoating in patient cells, as in the case of synaptojanin 1 KO synapses.
source: Our results also point to a defect in clathrin uncoating, as in the case of synaptojanin 1 KO synapses.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the accumulation of clathrin-coated vesicles shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The dramatic decrease in the number of actin comets upon the selective, pharmacologically-induced depletion of PI(4,5)P2 at the plasma membrane demonstrates that at least a large cohort of these comets are nucleated by endocytic vesicles.
source: The dramatic decrease in the number of these comets upon the selective, pharmacologically-induced depletion of PI(4,5)P2 at the plasma membrane demonstrates that at least a large cohort of these comets are nucleated by endocytic vesicles.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the data in Figure 6.

claim: The prominent impact of the lack of OCRL on total cellular PI(4,5)P2 levels in patient cells is reminiscent of the robust increase in brain levels of this phosphoinositide observed in the absence of synaptojanin 1.
source: The prominent impact of the lack of OCRL on total cellular PI(4,5)P2 levels in patient cells is reminiscent of the robust increase in brain levels of this phosphoinositide observed in the absence of synaptojanin 1 (Cremona et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Synaptojanin 1 and OCRL have partially overlapping functions, but with predominant roles at synapses and in non-neuronal cells, respectively.
source: We suggest that synaptojanin 1 and OCRL have partially overlapping functions, but with predominant roles at synapses and in non-neuronal cells, respectively.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation stated in the discussion.

claim: The newly discovered direct interaction of OCRL with SNX9 provides a new link between OCRL function and late-stage endocytic clathrin-coated pit nucleation.
source: The newly discovered direct interaction of OCRL with SNX9, a protein implicated in the transition from late stage clathrin-coated pits to free clathrin-coated vesicles, is of significant interest as it provides a new link between OCRL function and late-stage endocytic clathrin-coated pit nucleation.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the data in Figure 2.

claim: SNX9 is a member of a family of BAR domain-containing endocytic adaptors that help coordinate changes in bilayer curvature with reactions that occur as membranes progress along the endocytic pathway.
source: SNX9 is a member of a family of BAR domain-containing endocytic adaptors that help coordinate changes in bilayer curvature with reactions that occur as membranes progress along the endocytic pathway.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is established knowledge about SNX9.

claim: SNX9 is thought to have an important role in coupling clathrin coat maturation to actin nucleation.
source: Specifically, SNX9 is thought to have an important role in coupling clathrin coat maturation to actin nucleation (Yarar et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The observation that the knockdown of SNX9 decreases comet formation in patient cells supports a role for this protein in actin nucleation at clathrin-coated pits.
source: Our observation that the knockdown of SNX9 decreases comet formation in patient cells supports a role for this protein in actin nucleation at clathrin-coated pits.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The modular structure of SNX9 is ideally suited to mediate coordination between clathrin coat maturation and actin nucleation.
source: The modular structure of SNX9 is ideally suited to mediate this coordination.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is based on knowledge of SNX9 structure and function.

claim: SNX9 binds the plasma membrane with a PX-BAR domain module, which exhibits a preference for curved membranes enriched in PI(4,5)P2 and 3-phosphorylated phosphoinositides.
source: SNX9 binds the plasma membrane with a PX-BAR domain module, which exhibits a preference for curved membranes enriched in PI(4,5)P2 and 3-phosphorylated phosphoinositides (Gallop et al., 2013), clathrin via a 'clathrin-box' motif and AP-2 via an α-adaptin-binding motif (Lundmark and Carlsson, 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Through its SH3 domain, SNX9 binds and thus helps to activate both N-WASP to trigger actin nucleation, and dynamin to mediate fission.
source: Through its SH3 domain, SNX9 binds and thus helps to activate both N-WASP to trigger actin nucleation, and dynamin to mediate fission (Yarar et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The SH3 domain of SNX9 binds synaptojanin and also OCRL.
source: The SH3 domain of SNX9 binds synaptojanin and also OCRL, as we have demonstrated in this study.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the data in Figure 2.

claim: SNX9 is an attractive candidate to help bring together multiple factors involved in late-stage endocytosis.
source: Given that SNX9 is a protein dimer that is present in multiple copies at endocytic sites, SNX9 is an attractive candidate to help bring together all these factors.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation stated in the discussion.

claim: SNX9 was shown to act as an effector of PI(3,4)P2, which is generated at endocytic clathrin-coated pits by PI3KcIIα.
source: Recently, SNX9 was shown to act as an effector of PI(3,4)P2, which is generated at endocytic clathrin-coated pits by PI3KcIIα (Posor et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: 5-phosphatases such as OCRL and synaptojanin could directly contribute to PI(3,4)P2 production by dephosphorylation of PI(3,4,5)P3, or indirectly by generating PI4P from PI(4,5)P2 dephosphorylation.
source: In principle, 5-phosphatases such as OCRL and synaptojanin could directly contribute to PI(3,4)P2 production by dephosphorylation of PI(3,4,5)P3, or indirectly by generating PI4P, the PI3KcIIα substrate, from PI(4,5)P2 dephosphorylation (Posor et al., 2013; Schmid and Mettlen, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: SNX9 is recruited to coated pits prior to OCRL, and also in its absence.
source: However, SNX9 is recruited to coated pits prior to OCRL, and also in its absence.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the data in Figure 2E-G.

claim: The recruitment of OCRL at endocytic clathrin-coated pits coincides with the temporal recruitment signature of GAK.
source: Instead, the recruitment of OCRL at endocytic clathrin-coated pits coincides with the temporal recruitment signature of GAK (Taylor et al., 2011), which, like its homologue auxilin, is a cofactor for Hsc70 and thus a key player in the disassembly of the clathrin lattice after fission (Fotin et al., 2004; Massol et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Both OCRL and GAK peak after the clathrin fluorescence has started to diminish, as expected for proteins that mediate the shedding of the clathrin coat (GAK) and its adaptors (OCRL).
source: Both OCRL and GAK peak after the clathrin fluorescence has started to diminish, as expected for proteins that mediate the shedding of the clathrin coat (GAK) and its adaptors (OCRL).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the data in Figure 4D.

claim: The lack of GAK or auxilin results in endocytic defects in addition to the accumulation of clathrin-coated vesicles and empty clathrin cages.
source: Interestingly, the lack of GAK or auxilin results in endocytic defects in addition to the accumulation of clathrin-coated vesicles and empty clathrin cages (Lee et al., 2005, Yim et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The impairment of endocytosis due to lack of GAK or auxilin is thought to result from the sequestration of coat components on assembled lattices.
